items.title: Show HN: Fleetlayer – Framework for running many AI agents on multiple machines
items.summary: Hi HN! I ran into many problems when I started running lots of Claude Code sessions in parallel. I quickly ran out of usage, so I signed up for more Claude subs (which Anthropic terms allow.) Running so many different accounts meant that I couldn't use claude.ai artifacts anymore, because the browser has to be signed in to the same account in order to access them. It's a pain to keep signing in and out of accounts. This also broke the Claude in Chrome extension because that can also only be signed into a single account. Then I needed to manage AI agents that run on my laptop, a VM on my laptop, and multiple VMs on my home server. Claude Code has a messaging feature which is very useful, but agents can't see each other when they run on different machines. The Claude in Chrome extension only works for agents running on the same machine, so my remote agents couldn't help me with anything in the browser. It's really handy when they can access services that I'm already signed into. I set out to solve all of these problems and I ended up building Fleetlayer. It's a control plane and a node binary that you run on all your machines and VMs to connect them all together. It connects to Herdr (and other session managers soon), and it makes it possible for all your AI agents to message each other and access tools and resources on other machines (with permission.) It has a lot more features too: routing webhooks to agents, single sign-on, access rules, approvals, audit logs, remote terminals, remote browser sharing, centralized AI account sign-ins, session summaries, secrets management, and pages and apps (our own self-hosted version of claude.ai artifacts). A few ways to think of it: - The "Nextcloud" of claude.ai features (your own self-hosted artifacts, remote control, browser use, etc.) - The "Arch Linux" of OpenClaw (build your own agentic systems from swappable components and plugins) You can run everything on your laptop to try it out, then easily move any component to a different machine. If you want to build a proper production-grade home server to run many AI agents, Rust builds, and CI runners, I've also open sourced my own setup as a boilerplate IaC example repo. You just need to install Proxmox and then point your AI agent at the guide [1]. I'd be interested to know if anyone else would find Fleetlayer useful. Please let me know if you have any feature requests! [1] https://fleetlayer.ai/docs/guides/server-setup/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50675831 Points: 10 # Comments: 7

items.title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
items.summary: a ball will fall. trade on where it lands. I made this game! Some technical details: The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome. There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky. Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50667726 Points: 388 # Comments: 130
